summary: We develped a web page (ONLY during the 2 given days, as intended) for comparing NASA SPHEREx images of one sky position across time. It addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by letting a user play a detector in time order, sum the detectors of one observation, and subtract two epochs to see what moved or changed brightness. The public archive is hard to use for that comparison; this page opens a coordinate, lines the frames up, and keeps previous searches and cutouts in a local DB available when IRSA does not respond.
details:
SPHEREx from adsum is a web application for comparing NASA SPHEREx images of the same sky position across time. The user clicks a sky map or enters right ascension and declination, chooses the cutout size, and searches the SPHEREx releases published at the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). The application asks IRSA which frames cover that point, cuts each science image around the target, and orients every cutout north-up and east-left so the frames line up.

From one target the user can play the observations of a single detector in time order, sum the detectors that belong to the same observation, or subtract two epochs to see what changed. An AllWISE position from about 2010 is marked on the field as an earlier infrared reference. Objects saved by the user stay in the browser. The same search address can also return JSON for anyone who wants the list of frames without the page.

The intended impact is to make the public SPHEREx archive usable for the search this challenge asks for: objects that move or change brightness from one visit to the next. A student or researcher can open a coordinate and compare epochs before writing a pipeline. Saved frames remain available when IRSA does not respond.

Every successful search is stored in a local database. The next visit to that sky position shows those saved observations immediately, and they remain available if IRSA does not respond. A position that has never been searched, and that IRSA does not cover, is still reported as empty.

The project is written in Python and JavaScript, with HTML and CSS. Django serves the site. Astropy reads the FITS images, handles sky coordinates, and cuts them out. Astroquery talks to IRSA. NumPy and Pillow build the sum, the difference, and the PNG preview. Aladin Lite provides the sky map. Bootstrap and Google Fonts provide the interface. The six infrared detectors stay separate unless the user explicitly sums one observation, so wavelength is not mixed into a false detection.
